youtube.title: One WebRTC Stack, Sixteen Languages: Deleting the Mirrors | grpc-over-datachannels v0.44
youtube.description:
grpc-over-datachannels 0.44 deletes the mirrored Go and JavaScript WebRTC stacks. The Rust ICE/DTLS/SCTP cores — sans-io, pump-driven — are now the only implementations, consumed via C ABI (Go) and Wasm (JS, browsers, facades). Includes the three bugs the default flip exposed and the mirror-free conformance net.

Code: https://github.com/browser-grpc/grpc-over-datachannels
Release: https://github.com/browser-grpc/grpc-over-datachannels/releases/tag/v0.44.0
Blog: https://c100k.blogspot.com/

Built with Fish Audio

scenes.heading: Deleting the Mirrors
scenes.sub: One WebRTC stack for sixteen languages
scenes.say: This project used to have three WebRTC stacks: one in Rust, and hand-mirrored copies in Go and JavaScript. The new release deletes two of them, and here is why, and what broke along the way.

scenes.heading: Three stacks, one drift
bullets: ICE, DTLS, and SCTP implemented in Rust, Go, and JavaScript
Mirrors kept in sync by discipline and a conformance suite
v0.32: a reassembly wedge existed in exactly one stack
scenes.say: Three implementations of the same protocols, synchronized by discipline. It already failed once: a fragment reassembly bug wedged ordered delivery in one stack while the other two were fine. State machines that must not drift should not exist three times.

scenes.say: The mirrors are gone. The Rust original is the only stack left. Go consumes it through a C A B I. JavaScript consumes the same code compiled to WebAssembly. Browsers and the generated facade languages ride the Rust bridge runtime.

scenes.heading: Sans-io: pump-driven cores
bullets: No sockets, no threads inside ICE / DTLS / SCTP
Datagrams and candidates cross as data; clocks are injected
Hosts own I/O: Go cgo seams, JS factories, Peer as driver
scenes.say: This only works because the cores are sans I O: pump-driven state machines. Datagrams, candidates, and credentials cross the boundary as data. Hosts own the sockets. That is what lets one implementation run in a Go process, a Node process, and a browser tab.

scenes.heading: One call, end to end
scenes.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 1500 620' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' font-family='DejaVu Sans, sans-serif'><text x='250' y='60' fill='#e8ecf6' font-size='34' text-anchor='middle'>Browser (Wasm cores)</text><text x='1250' y='60' fill='#e8ecf6' font-size='34' text-anchor='middle'>Node (Wasm cores)</text><line x1='250' y1='80' x2='250' y2='560' stroke='#3a4a6e' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='1250' y1='80' x2='1250' y2='560' stroke='#3a4a6e' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M250 140 L1250 140' stroke='#6ea8ff' stroke-width='3'/><text x='750' y='128' fill='#aab6d3' font-size='28' text-anchor='middle'>ICE checks → nomination</text><path d='M250 240 L1250 240' stroke='#6ea8ff' stroke-width='3'/><text x='750' y='228' fill='#aab6d3' font-size='28' text-anchor='middle'>DTLS flights → established</text><path d='M250 340 L1250 340' stroke='#9fe8a9' stroke-width='3'/><text x='750' y='328' fill='#aab6d3' font-size='28' text-anchor='middle'>SCTP INIT → association</text><path d='M250 440 L1250 440' stroke='#9fe8a9' stroke-width='3'/><text x='750' y='428' fill='#aab6d3' font-size='28' text-anchor='middle'>DCEP channel → gRPC frames</text><path d='M1250 520 L250 520' stroke='#ffb454' stroke-width='3'/><text x='750' y='508' fill='#aab6d3' font-size='28' text-anchor='middle'>echo response</text></svg>
scenes.say: One echo call, end to end. I C E checks nominate a pair. D T L S flights establish the session. S C T P associates, a channel opens, and g R P C frames flow. Every arrow on both sides is the same Rust code.

scenes.heading: The honest cost
bullets: FFI tax measured: ~311 ns vs 173 ns per 200-byte delivery
Paid for one conformance-tested implementation, not speed
Echo path today: ~8,300 msgs/s at 0.36 ms mean RTT
scenes.say: The shared core is not free. Crossing the F F I costs about three hundred eleven nanoseconds per message, against one seventy-three for the old mirror. We measured it, published it, and paid it anyway: that is the price of one tested implementation instead of three that can drift.

scenes.heading: Live: mux_bench on the consolidated stack
scenes.say: Here is the benchmark live: eight pairs handshaking, two thousand echoes blasted through the mux, and ping-pong at a third of a millisecond. Same numbers as before the mirrors died.

scenes.heading: Bugs the flip exposed
bullets: Wasm DTLS pump killed by JavaScript `undefined` (all 8 stress dials)
64-deep demux queue → retransmit storms on MiB messages
Registry test racing two clients on one transport (9m56s CI hang)
Public Go/browser/interop CI red until the cores were built first
scenes.say: Flipping the defaults earned its keep. A Wasm adapter confused undefined with null and killed every D T L S pump under load. A shallow queue turned burst loss into retransmit storms. A test raced two clients on one transport and hung C I for ten minutes. Each one shipped with a regression test.

scenes.heading: Oracles without mirrors
bullets: OpenSSL differentials for DTLS; shared SCTP vectors everywhere
ICE consent/trickle suites against the core
make ci-status: every generated repo green on v0.44.0
scenes.say: Deleting a second implementation deletes your differential oracle, so the conformance net is mirror-free by design: Open S S L differentials, shared vectors, and full suites that only have the Rust path to run on. One command sweeps every generated repository's C I. It is all green.

scenes.heading: One stack, maintained once
bullets: Blog post: link in the description
make ci-status — try the sweep yourself
scenes.say: About forty-four hundred lines of mirrored Go and JavaScript are gone. One WebRTC stack, maintained once, spoken in sixteen languages. The code and the release are on GitHub. Links are in the description.
